lines: Some hedges showed twice the volume and twice the money they were worth, and said the deals and the balance disagreed about the account. The deals had been recorded a second time on 19 September, when the way an account is referred to changed. Installing this puts the record right and works the figures out again. Your data is copied before anything touches it, as it is on every update.

The product refuses to arm when the plan already carries a hedge, whether the product placed it or you opened it yourself in MetaTrader, and on any of the plan's accounts. The line beside the button says why it is grey.

Sizing a hedge counts what the broker account has already put behind the positions it is holding. Sizing one on a broker that is already carrying another plan's hedge no longer reports a margin level the broker would never agree with.
The target no longer reads wrong in points or in money for the first moment after the calculator opens.
Positions with no counterpart and an account's ledger fill as you scroll rather than putting you through numbered pages, and Positions with no counterpart can be narrowed to one account.
A licence that runs out while a hedge is open no longer locks you out of it. You can still see what is open, close it, disarm it, or cancel an order that is waiting.
You can enter a new licence key from the About page before the old one expires. It tells you what that key covers before you use it.
Record what you pay to run this, starting with your licence. You choose whether it comes off your result as a step of its own.
A target at the pass point clears what the trade really costs to open and close. It used to allow for one commission where two are charged, and for none at all on an account that had not traded yet.
Switching a trade between buy and sell moves the stop and the target to the right side of the entry. They used to stay where they were, which swapped what each one meant.
The Hedges page narrows to one prop account.
A terminal you make appears on the Terminals tab straight away. You can also correct what a plan cost after recording it.

The product refuses to arm while the plan already holds a position, including one you opened yourself in MetaTrader. The wait before firing counts down where you can see it, you can cancel it, and the calculator is locked once a hedge is armed.
A plan shows what is standing on its funded accounts, and your share of it after the split, beside what the plan has cost you. A plan that reads down while its account is up now says why.
One terminal that stops answering no longer holds up the others. A terminal the product cannot read says why, rather than quietly slowing everything down.

When a terminal changes account, the product notices and points itself at the new one within half a minute. It used to go on driving the old one. Every failing check that a restart can clear now offers the button that does it, and a terminal the product starts comes back the way it was running.

The badge in the corner counts the terminals actually being driven, not the ones with a route chosen. A terminal driven through its own windows can now be started and set up from its row, which until now only a terminal on the expert route could. An account's bar carries its balance on the marker, and puts each distance under the end it is measured to.

The hedge ratio counts what the broker has already taken in on a stage as money that stage can spend. It holds at the price you named, rather than falling every time the account loses: on a $25,000 Class B with $350 set aside for the stage, one hedge was enough to drop the suggestion from 14.00% to 10.99%.

The risk figure under the calculator's rail is what the position really risks, not what the sizing was asked for. The two come apart whenever you set the lots by hand, and the figure turns red when it is past what your plan allows. Moving a level on one leg now carries only what you choose. A stop still moves the other leg's target and a target moves nothing, so trailing a broker target by hand no longer moves your prop stop. Four switches for it under Settings, Driving the terminals. The calculator also opens with the entry following the market.

**One journal on every computer you trade from.** Turn it on in Settings, Journals, and your record is kept the same on each machine through a hidden folder in your own Google Drive. It is sealed with a passphrase only you know: nobody here ever sees it and nobody can recover it. Each machine still reads only its own terminals, and nothing about you or your machines reaches us. The page says which Google account the copy goes to and how much room that account has left, so a Drive that is filling up is something you hear about before it stops the copy rather than after.

**When two of your computers change the same thing, you decide which is right.** Both versions are kept and the question is put to you; neither is thrown away on its own. Your answer then reaches every machine rather than only the one you gave it on. A computer that already holds a record of its own can join and keep it, and whatever only that one had is carried across. Sources lists the machines sharing the journal, what each is running and when it last spoke. One that is gone for good can be forgotten. The header says how it stands and speaks only when something needs you: a computer you have switched off is not a warning, and the Journals page says which of them has not caught up yet.

**Hedging from two computers at once is now safe.** Arming checks your other machines first, so two of them can never hedge the same plan, and the refusal says which one got there first. The checks count what those machines already have at risk on the same accounts, so two of them cannot between them break the firm's daily limit or close each other's hedge out. A hedge belongs to the machine that armed it: only that machine can fire it, move it or close it, and the others show it with that machine's name beside it. Stopping automatic actions stops them everywhere, and the status says where it was stopped from.

**The trailing stop is the desk expert's now, and it is off until you turn it on.** Four rules to choose from in Settings. It follows the broker leg only, so nothing is ever moved on a prop account, and the shadow stop that used to close a leg early is gone. What each rule did on eight months of real bars is written down rather than guessed at.

**Every screen that reports a hedge separates what you chose from what it cost.** Leaving one leg running after its partner closed is a decision, and it is now reported as one instead of arriving as a cost you never paid. It is told apart from an accidental parting on evidence: a stop or target seen to move before the other leg closed, or a gap wider than your own review threshold. Reports say whether running on has paid you: how often you did it, how often it worked, what it earned against what it gave back, and how much of what was on the table you kept. Every position now records the best it was ever worth while it was open, which is what that last figure is measured against.

**Slippage is measured against the price the order actually asked for.** A close triggered by a stop, a target or a stop out is the one fill in this product with a requested price to compare against, so it is exact rather than an estimate. The levels come from the order rather than the deal, which is where they have always been; the fifty-six entry levels this product had stored as zero were read from the wrong record.

**The hedges page counts every settled hedge.** It counted only the ones nobody had left a question on, so a closed hedge waiting to be read through was missing from the page's own total while every other screen included it. Money that was earned weeks ago no longer appears the day somebody presses Accept.

**An instrument your terminal is not watching is no longer armed against.** It has no price and no stop rules there, and those zeros used to read as permission. The product now puts the instrument into Market Watch itself where the desk expert is attached, says so on the arming checks when it does, and asks you to add it by hand where no expert is there to do it.

**The accounts table says who each account is registered to**, and Accounts, Hedges and Plans can be narrowed to one person's accounts. The name stays on your own machines and is never in a journal you export.

**Four things about the shared journal that went wrong and no longer do.** Taking a copy failed while the product was reading your terminals. A change being read at the moment its file moved was skipped instead of read again on the next look. A computer switched off for a long time started again from scratch on every look once it came back, rather than once. And changing the passphrase sent your whole record to Drive a second time. Times on that page are shown in your own clock too, matching the rest of the product.

**The application installs and runs again on older computers.** A library that arrives with the MetaTrader package had raised what it needs to an instruction set no processor before 2008 has, so on an older machine the installation finished and the application then refused to start, every time, with a message blaming something that was not the problem. It is back to what it has always needed, which every 64-bit computer since 2004 has. The same applies to a virtual machine whose host presents an older processor.

**If a computer really is too old for it, the installer says so before it installs anything** rather than leaving you with a copy that cannot start, and it says what to change when the machine is a virtual one.

**A funded account is no longer reported as having gone through its drawdown floor because a terminal answered with nothing while it was starting.** One such reading was spending the account's entire allowance, 833% of it, and the plan asked you to confirm it was over while the account was in profit and trading. The same reading no longer counts against what you have left today either, and it is kept out of the balances that prove a hedge's result.

**A plan is drawn as a straight rail of its accounts, and each stop says what it did to your money.** Green where a challenge passed or an account paid out, red where one was lost, brass on the account being traded now, and the line between two stops wears the colour of what came before it. The account you are trading has a panel of its own under the rail, with its standing at full size, and clicking any stop takes you to that account's own hedges. A chain of nine accounts reads as easily as one.

**The hedge calculator sizes a funded account whose plan has already earned its cost back**, instead of refusing with "the broker side cannot be sized". On a funded account the rail, the split line and "each win nets" now use the same profit share as the valuation, which is the share your firm pays on the plan's next payout: 90% on a seventh Class B account, not the 75% of the first. A refund already recorded is no longer added again under "from payout one".

**Money made on a funded account is valued at the share your firm actually pays on it**, everywhere the calculator shows what a trade would return. On a challenge account, a hedge's result is what moved in your broker account and nothing else, because a challenge balance is never money you can withdraw. What a lot costs in margin is read from the terminal instead of being typed in.

**A funded account is no longer reported as blown because of a reading taken while its terminal was still starting.** If a plan of yours was asking you to confirm it was over, it will stop. A funded plan whose chain has earned its cost back is told so, instead of "the profit has reached the $0.00 you set", and an account that has gone quiet past the firm's limit is told how long, rather than "0 days left". The budget on a stage that has already passed or failed can no longer be edited.

**The calculator's boxes take what you type.** The risk in money can be typed into again: entering 740 used to leave the box reading $7.02, because it reformatted itself between keystrokes, and a figure typed into any money box is no longer rewritten under you while you are still writing it. Typing is much faster, and the entry price takes the number of decimals the instrument actually quotes to.

**The calculator says where the money goes before you arm.** The account picker and the bar above Arm both name the account each leg will be placed on, and that bar keeps the same arrangement whatever width the calculator is at.

**Arming asks for your agreement where you are.** On a real account it opens a dialog that names the account and says what agreeing permits, where it used to refuse the press and send you to a terminal row that had no such button. And when the broker's margin figure is missing, arming now says to put the instrument in the broker terminal's Market Watch, which is what makes the figure appear, instead of pointing at a Sources box that no longer exists.

**A terminal or an account can be removed from Sources.** Removing a terminal also removes its reads from the Evidence tab and your agreement to restart it, so adding it again asks before it closes anything; the accounts and deals it imported are kept. Removing an account takes everything it brought in, shows you what would go before anything does, and is remembered, so the next read of its terminal does not bring it back. The Accounts tab lists what is being skipped, with a button to read it again.

**The Sources page remembers which tab you were on**, its tabs can be linked to the way the Settings tabs already could, and they have room around them. The Plans page no longer flashes "No plan yet" while the plans are still being fetched.

**The licence is confirmed about every six hours.** After a day without reaching the internet the application says so, instead of after three weeks; if it cannot reach the licence list for two days it locks, and connecting once clears it. A licence can now be issued for a set number of days: when one runs out the application says so on a screen of its own, with the day it ran until, and a licence with a week or less to run says so while you can still do something about it. Your figures and both exports are never affected, and licences issued before this release run until 30 September 2026.

**On a funded account, the profit you have made is now valued at the share a payout pays you** rather than at what the challenge allowance cost. A winning funded hedge was being reported as a loss: one worth $297.12 on the prop side against $98.64 at the broker read as -$52.21, and it is +$124.20. The share follows your plan's ladder, so a second funded account is valued at the rate the firm actually pays on it. The break-even ratio is unchanged and still means what it says, and the figure a payout is measured against now follows what reaching the account has cost instead of staying at whatever it was the day the account arrived.

**The desk on your chart has tabs now, and one of them lists what is open.** Positions shows every position on the instrument with its stop, its size and what it is worth, and lets you take one into the chain or release it without touching the others. Settings holds the rest: the theme, the colours, and which way the trailing stop follows.

**The desk draws the chart's lines itself.** You can drag the chain's stop and its target the way you drag anything else, and a position you gave a level of its own gets a line of its own with its ticket on it. Each line says what reaching it is worth: the money, the share of the balance, the distance in points, and what the chain stands to make against what it risks. The area between the stop and the target is shaded, so you can see both at a glance. Dragging on the average line starts a new line instead of moving the average, dragging a waiting entry no longer moves a position's stop that happens to sit at the same price, and the figures keep up when you move the chart.

**A stop or target you set yourself is kept.** On every position in the chain, and on the ones you open afterwards. A position you closed by hand now counts as part of what the chain has banked, so the average line moves by what you took off and the bar shows it beside your open result.
**You can size a trade by what you are willing to lose.** The desk's volume box takes lots, a share of the balance, or an amount of money, and always shows the lots it comes to.

**The trailing stop keeps running after the price reaches your target.** The target moves ahead with the trade instead of closing it, and the stop is what ends the trade. There is also a second way to trail, which follows the chart's own range below the highest bar rather than sitting a spread behind the best price. You choose between them on the desk's Settings tab.

**The desk sets your chart up when it loads, and gives it back when it comes off.** What the chart shows, candles, the newest bar at the middle of the screen, and a vertical scale you can drag instead of one that springs back. Settings has a button to do it again, and a dark or a light theme for the chart. With a theme on, the desk wears colours made for it: its border is the chart's grid, its text the chart's own, and its green and red the candles'. Turn the theme off and your usual colours come back, exactly as they were.
**Your desk settings survive an expert update**, the panel stays above anything drawn on the chart, and its box and lines are readable on a dark chart.
**Setting a terminal up no longer leaves the desk unable to talk to the product.** The settings file it saved was written in a way that sent the desk looking for a connection that does not exist.

**The expert is asked for where it is used.** A hedge whose prop leg you open yourself no longer asks you to attach TradeDesk in the prop terminal. It is always needed in the broker terminal, where it guards the leg even if the product stops running, and in the prop terminal only when the product places that leg through it.

**The calculator says what a trade costs to get into, in your own money.** The broker's charges in full, and the prop account's at the ratio the two legs actually trade at, because winning a prop dollar back costs you that much. A funded account still counts the whole charge.

**The calculator shows which way the trade goes.** The side is in the colour of the header, the footer and the Arm button, so a hedge set up the wrong way round is visible before it is armed. The figures carry colour where it means something as well: each leg's side, the hedge ratio, money that is a gain or a loss, and the stop and target boxes.

**The calculator's entry field works again, and lines up.** NOW and the follow button do something when pressed, and they stay put when the up and down arrows appear beside them. Typing a new entry price moves the stop and a target you typed with it and keeps the distances, where before an entry typed past the stop left the trade with no stop at all. The field lines up with the stop and the target, those two labels are red and green again, and gold is marked as the recommended instrument in the picker and listed first among the ones both terminals watch.

**A leg left standing on its own is closed.** If one side of a hedge cannot be opened, the side that did open comes off immediately instead of being left there alone. A position you opened by hand is never closed this way.

**Arming warns you when a market is about to close**, an hour before by default and adjustable in Settings. Refusing inside the last fifteen minutes is unchanged. The terminals are read every fifteen seconds now, and every five while a position is open, both on the Settings page.

**Two things on the hedge ledger.** A column filter works every time rather than only the first: choosing a second account after a first found nothing used to find nothing either, and clearing the filter did not bring the whole ledger back. And in a narrow window the first column no longer has its text cut in half when you scroll sideways.

**Instruments whose name carries a longer tag are recognised again.** Some brokers add a word to the end of a symbol rather than a letter or two: IFC Markets writes gold `XAUUSD.BOOK`. The application read a tag of one or two characters and not a word, so on those accounts every trade under the name was skipped. There were no positions, no hedges, and the calculator offered no instruments and said no prop account had been read, on an account whose balance was on the screen beside it. Nothing was lost while that was happening: your trades were still recorded, and they come back with everything built on them the first time this version reads your terminal.

**And where a name genuinely cannot be placed, the calculator says so.** It used to send you to add a MetaTrader terminal, which is no help when the terminal is running and the account is read. It now tells you what happened and points at Settings, Catalogues, where you can say what the name means. One answer there settles every trade under it.

**A broker trade is no longer counted against two plans at once.** If one broker account hedged more than one prop account, a single ticket could be attributed twice. Everything built on the broker side was affected: your realised cash, each plan's result, the cost pages and the export. It is corrected, and the figures now add up to what your accounts actually traded. Nothing you recorded was changed; the same trades are simply counted once.

**The hedge ratio comes from money you name, not from a setting.** When you record a plan you now say what you are willing to spend at the broker to pass each stage, and the ratio follows from that: what is left of the budget over what is left to the target. The plan's chain shows each stage's budget and how much of it the hedging has used, and you can change a stage's figure from there. The old ratio setting is gone, and the Catalogue tab now holds only what the firms publish.

**A funded account has a control of its own.** There is no pass point to aim at, so instead of a ratio you name what you are willing to spend at the broker over the account. The rail marks the band where that cost comes back whichever way the account goes, whether it reaches a payout or is lost, and underneath it says what the broker pays, what reaches you from the first payout, what the broker keeps if the account dies, and how many accounts it takes to earn the cost back and double it.

**On a funded account, the profit share and the waiting periods follow the plan.** Your firm pays a bigger share on later payouts, and an account it issues after a payout used to start that ladder again: 75% where the terms say 80%, with the first payout's waiting period offered to you a second time after you had already served it. The share, the waiting period and the trading-day count are the plan's now. The withdrawal figure also follows what reaching it cost, including the refund that arrives after the account does.

**Today's drawdown floor is measured from the balance the day opened at.** It used to be measured from whatever the balance happened to be the first time the application looked, which on a day that had already traded was the wrong figure. It is read from the account's own deals now. The calculator also says which floor a trade would spend, the day's or the whole allowance.

**When you are trading a challenge to fail, the target can go at the balance you bought the account at.** Beside each choice is what your broker account can carry against it, which is the reason to choose between them: the nearer target caps what a winning trade costs you, so a smaller broker account can carry a larger hedge.

**The calculator shows what a trade costs before you take it.** Each terminal's spread in money, its commission, what each side comes to and what both come to together, against what the trade risks, so a stop too tight to be worth trading is visible before it is placed. It also says what your ratio will actually come to once both spreads are paid. Both outcome boxes can be read backwards: name what the broker leg should return, or what you are willing to pay if the prop account wins, and the ratio and both lot sizes are worked out from it.

**Every hedge says how closely it mirrored.** The ratio it was placed at, the ratio that arrived, and where the difference went. A hedge whose broker side was several tickets draws each of them, with its own entry, exit and size.

**The trading desk on the chart can look after positions it did not open.** Press Adopt and it takes on a position you opened yourself, with the same trailing stop and the same protection as one it placed. Several faults in the desk are fixed as well: it no longer reports chains that are not open, its labels keep their last words, a stop or target you move on one leg always reaches the other, and an order left resting on the chart is cancelled at the broker rather than only removed from the screen.

**The reports have moved to one place each.** The Overview now carries the cash ledger and both growth charts beside the figures they explain, and the Plans page is the plans: the cards, the chain, and the one thing each needs. The Excel export has a sheet for your plans and one for every purchase, refund and payout, and each hedge row says which account and which plan it belongs to. The per-pair cash column no longer charges every pair the whole portfolio's fees, so its rows can be added up.

**Setting a terminal up is clearer, and arming says more.** The Sources page marks which way of driving a terminal suits the kind of account it holds and says why, a terminal carrying an older desk offers to update it, and a new portable terminal always gets the shortcut that starts it in portable mode. You can also say what a lot costs in margin on a broker account: the application will not arm a hedge without that figure, it can only measure it while something is open, and a brand new account has nothing to measure yet.

**A great many smaller things.** A page with nothing on it says so and stops instead of drawing an empty copy of itself. The cash ledger names the plan each movement belongs to, and dates purchases and payouts when the money moved rather than when you typed them in. A stage that spends more than its budget says by how much. Percentages say what they are a share of. A hedge is only queried when two positions really were open on the prop account at once. And the floating calculator no longer covers the buttons on the last card.

**A hedge can now wait at a price.** Arm one at a price the market has not reached and press Wait here. Both sides are placed as orders that sit on their own servers, at the same point, each with its stop and its target already on it. Nothing is open while it waits. Whichever side the market takes first, the other goes straight to the market to answer it, so you are never left holding one leg. If the market takes both at once, that is one hedge and it is recorded as one.

**A waiting hedge can be moved, and called off from either end.** Drag its entry line on the chart in the terminal and both orders move together, keeping the distances you set. Press Cancel on the strip and both come off their servers. Settings holds how long one may wait before it gives up on its own, and it waits indefinitely unless you say otherwise.

**It works on both kinds of terminal.** Until now a hedge could only be left waiting on a terminal running TradeDesk. A terminal driven through its own Order window can now do it too: placed, moved to another price, and called off the same way.

**Both sides of a hedge now leave together.** They used to be prepared one after the other and could reach their brokers as much as four seconds apart, which is four seconds of a hedge that is not hedged. Everything slow now happens before anything is sent, so the two orders go within a millisecond of each other. Measured on real terminals: between a tenth and a seventh of a millisecond, whichever way each terminal is driven.
**When one side of a waiting hedge is taken, the other now follows in about two seconds** instead of fourteen. Most of that fourteen was the application looking in the wrong place for its own order.

**The record says exactly when each order went.** Open a hedge and its history shows the moment each of the two orders left, so you can see for yourself that both sides went together rather than taking our word for it.

**A plan carries one hedge at a time.** That holds however the position arrives, including when you open it yourself in the terminal, and it counts every account the plan has held rather than only the current one. Two different plans still run their own hedges side by side, untouched by each other.
**A position you open yourself is hedged as it fills**, rather than up to thirty seconds later when the next pass came round.

**The calculator says why it will not arm.** Press Arm on a plan it cannot accept and the reason now appears and stays on the screen: which price is on the wrong side of which, or what about the machine is in the way. It used to leave the button exactly as it was and say nothing at all.

**Driving a terminal through its own Order window is reliable now.** Arming used to fail about every other attempt on a slow terminal, with a message that named no cause. Several other faults on that route were found and fixed at the same time: an order the market had taken being reported as a cancel that failed, a price the market crossed while the window was opening being refused with a message about a button, and closing a position taking five seconds where it now takes under two.
**A terminal you drive by hand is never sent an order.** That is what driving it by hand means, and the one place it could have happened is closed.
**A way of driving a terminal that could never work for that account is greyed out on the Sources page**, with the reason, instead of being accepted and refused later when you arm.
**When Windows refuses an action on a terminal, the hedge's row says what happened in words** rather than showing an error nobody can read.
**Part of a leg closing is no longer treated as the leg closing.** The hedge says what happened and leaves both positions where they are.

**Smaller things.** One terminal that cannot be read no longer stops the others being read, and the header no longer claims nothing has been read for days while it is reading. The list of terminals keeps up with what the application does to them. Choosing an instrument only one of your two accounts trades says so, instead of blaming the account. Terminals the application starts stay open when it closes, with your charts and your account where you left them. Closing a hedge from the strip is written down like every other order. And the calculator can be opened by address and its size suggestions reached from the keyboard.
